We demonstrate the convergence of a specific ergodic average associated with the zero system of Hecke-Maass newforms at prime frequency multiples, and link this result to the distribution of Landau-Siegel zeros within the critical plane of these functions.

We have adapted the relational Hoare calculus to accommodate a quantum program's behavior, defined by expectation values of observation operators. By linking the relational hoare calculus with the behavior definition, we can establish a sound and complete proof system for validating the correctness of quantum programs under metric preservation. Notably, this proof system incorporates a complete set of rules for both classical and quantum programs.

The rapid transmission of contagious diseases is frequently intensified by a single high-transmission-event, a super-spreader occurrence. This phenomenon, which can result in a significant surge in new cases, has been observed during outbreaks of pandemic proportions, such as the widespread of the 1918 influenza and the 2020 SARS-CoV-2 transmission. A new mathematical model has been developed to examine the impact of super-spreader events on the acceleration of an epidemic. This model, which takes into account various levels of super-spreader transmission, can be applied to a variety of epidemiological scenarios, including those affected by community transmission, and measures the epidemic's progression, as well as the transmission of the virus within the super-spreader population. A critical analysis of the model's parameters has been conducted, revealing that even a modest level of super-spreader transmission can lead to a significant increase in the epidemic's size. This has significant implications for public health policy, highlighting the importance of identifying and isolating super-spreaders promptly in order to slow the spread of an epidemic.

Letting $\mathcal{X}$ denote the space of complex topological vector fields on a noncompact manifold $M$, we investigate codiskcyclic collections of operators acting on $\mathcal{X}$ and determine their characterizing properties. It is also demonstrated that these collections are inherently associative and commutative in nature.

The paper addresses the problem of bias in vector magnetic field maps, particularly in estimating the component perpendicular to the line-of-sight, using chromatic inversions in spectroscopic data. It is demonstrated that there is indeed a source of bias stemming from the application of linear combinations of spectra, which can result in inaccurate measurements of $B_\perp$. A correction method is proposed to mitigate this effect by utilizing a model of the spectroscopic response that incorporates a calibration of the inversions. This approach is tested using synthetic data and proven effective in reducing $B_\perp$ bias to nearly insignificant levels. Furthermore, the paper explores the connection between $B_\perp$ bias and fill-factor estimation, revealing that a decrease in $B_\perp$ bias corresponds to an overestimation of fill factors. Consequently, a modified procedure is suggested to alleviate $B_\perp$ bias by incorporating a second-generation contrast parameter in the inversions. This leads to an improved description of magnetized granulation and, in turn, more accurate measurements of vector magnetic fields.

A type of neural network known as complex-weighted neural networks has been proposed as a viable option for modeling two-types of local spins in the Hubbard model using sign-free parameters. By converting complex-weighted neural networks to their equivalent real-valued forms, we demonstrate that certain complex-valued architectures result in models that inherently pose no "Hubbard Sign Dilemma". Through numerical simulations, it was found that a specific network with a specific number of layers can achieve accurate results for ground state energies and magnetization lengths within the Hubbard model, even when using large numbers of two-types of local spins.

Given any non-recursive formal sequence type, we can establish its complexity within a specific free group framework. Similarly, the complexity of another free group-based sequence can be determined using another defined structure. In this context, defined structures serve as equivalents to recognition languages. The complexity of these sequences is calculated by measuring the length of their shortest defining formulas. It has been previously demonstrated that natural homomorphisms preserve the complexity of these sequences. Here, we prove that both natural and unnatural homomorphisms also preserve their entropy. In addition to homomorphisms, we examine how alterations to a free group basis affect complexity and entropy. Specifically, we investigate how changing from a free group basis generates complexity and entropy, and to what extent this new complexity and entropy are equivalent to their original forms.

By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to boost the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with a focus on models like T0 and FLAN.
We introduce a novel, unsupervised retrieval-augmented method called RECAST, which leverages previously encountered language data to facilitate cross-task generalization.
The proposed method combines three key components: a query suitable for retrieving relevant language patterns, a scoring function to compare retrieved instances, and a knowledge filter to eliminate misleading examples.
We evaluate RECAST on multiple unsupervised cross-task generalization benchmarks, showing significant improvements over existing methods and a strong baseline built using monolingual data.

Differentially Private Deep Learning models have gained significant traction due to their potential to prevent member data breaches and safeguard sensitive information. However, there is a major challenge related to the optimization process, which significantly hinders the performance of these models. The issue arises from the fact that stochastic gradient descent, a fundamental algorithm for training neural networks, requires the selection of several key parameters, which necessarily increases the risk of data breaches. To mitigate this risk, researchers have proposed various differentially private versions of the ADMM algorithm, but they have limitations, particularly in relation to the scalability for large datasets. In contrast, the proposed method introduces a novel way to reduce the impact of hyperparameters on data breaches by applying a non-uniform random perturbation to the gradients. The experimental results indicate that this proposed method successfully mitigates the risk of data breaches while simultaneously enhancing the accuracy of differentially private deep learning models.

A permutation $ \sigma $ in $ S_n $ is considered complex if it induces a complex permutation on the set of involutions in $ S_n $, meaning its disjoint cycle structure does not consist of pairs of transpositions. We investigate the prospect of constructing a boolean function $ f $ such that $ f(1, \ldots, n) $ represents a complex permutation structure, along with a discussion on related themes.

We applied an advanced statistical approach to analyze the composition of 18,378 stars in the Milky Way disk using a vast amount of spectroscopic data. By leveraging a two-component model that accounts for absorption features caused by elements formed by capture and fusion, we were able to pinpoint the sources of variability in elemental abundances across the galaxy. According to our findings, there are fluctuations in the abundance of elements created through capture, particularly as we move towards the galaxy's center. Furthermore, we discovered a relationship between the abundance of these elements and the rate of fusion, indicating that there may be an underlying pattern of metal scattering. Additionally, we found that the distribution of elements formed by fusion is not entirely uniform, with certain regions exhibiting enhanced abundances of certain elements. These regions could be the result of specific events such as stellar mergers or massive stellar explosions.

The rapid spread of COVID-19 in China led to severe consequences, and online rumors significantly exacerbated the issue. To combat this problem, the Chinese government launched a special rumor-refuting website, providing official responses to address circulating information. However, the effectiveness of this initiative remains unclear. To explore the mechanism behind the dissemination of online rumors and assess the government's response, we collected real-time data from Sina Weibo, the most popular Chinese microblog platform, along with related statistical information. Our findings reveal that the rapid transmission of online rumors can be attributed to factors such as user trust, education level, and the presence of authoritative figures in their social networks. Furthermore, we found that the government's response and subsequent discussion about a particular issue could significantly reduce the belief in that rumor. Nonetheless, the relationship between the dissemination of rumors and user interactions revealed a complex interplay, with conditional analysis indicating that the government's response is more likely to prevent the further diffusion of rumors when users have low confidence in them, whereas interactions among users tend to accelerate the spread of rumors in various contexts.

A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies has been developed, leveraging the characteristics of planetary nebulae over a range of scales without requiring individual nebulae distances. Pioneering this method are researchers from the Fornax3D and CALYPSO collaborations, utilizing comprehensive data on planetary nebulae ejections. By synthesizing and analyzing extensive information on planetary nebulae with various sizes and shapes, a automated technique has been developed to calculate the average distance to galaxies based on planetary nebulae with radial velocities within a specific range. Applying this technique to galaxies in the Fornax cluster, a well-studied and reliable standard, yields a distance measurement to these galaxies of 48.75 megaparsecs with an associated error of 1.44 megaparsecs. This novel technique has been utilized successfully to measure the distance to galaxies across a range of scales and luminosities, demonstrating its utility and accuracy.

Every day, hospitals around the world gather vast amounts of physiological data from their patients, leading to an escalating interest in conducting statistical analyses to provide better medical diagnoses. These analyses involve complex computations on significant datasets, necessitating high-performance data processing systems that can balance efficiency and simplicity. To address the limitations of existing data processing solutions, we present \emph{LifeStream}, a robust stream processing engine specifically designed to handle physiological data efficiently. LifeStream optimizes performance while providing intuitive temporal query language support, thus striking a balance between ease of programming and computational speed. Furthermore, LifeStream exhibits superior performance, outperforming other leading stream processing engines and hand-tuned numerical libraries by up to $7.5\times$ and $3.2\times$ respectively, on realistic datasets and workload simulations.

This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in higher dimensional space, do not fit the classification of Bertrand curves except in two-dimensional Euclidean space. A new category, called the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve, is defined to fill this gap and its characteristics are identified for curves in four-dimensional Euclidean space.

When utilizing deep learning for a binary classification task with an imbalanced dataset, numerous methods have been developed to address the issue of class imbalance. Most research focuses on selecting the optimal robustness and calibration tradeoff for confidence-based models, without considering the underlying statistics of the data. This study investigates the fundamental principles of loss function optimization for deep learning with imbalanced data and explores three key concepts: the relationship between thresholding and loss function, the impact of normalized losses, and the effect of strong versus weak constraints on classification. Through theoretical and empirical analyses, we gained insights into the behavior of deep learning models under different loss functions and data distributions. Subsequently, we developed a strategy for selecting optimal loss functions based on the underlying data characteristics. This approach allows us to leverage the benefits of normalized losses, confidence scoring, and calibration techniques. Our proposed method achieves superior performance in comparison to conventional techniques, as demonstrated by the experimental results.

This research focuses on simulating and understanding the thermal and mechanical effects of crystalline material structure development during polymer deformation. To achieve this, a non-isothermal finite element method was combined with a Lagrange multiplier technique to ensure incompressibility, and a user material interface was utilized to integrate numerical simulations with material models, including strain-induced crystallization and parabolic lubrication. The results of these simulations were compared with experimental data, revealing that the proposed method effectively captures temperature and stress distributions during crystallization. Furthermore, this approach was applied to analyze the influence of mechanical loading, thermal properties, and initial microstructure properties on crystalline material structure development.

To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet nematic superconductivity, we computationally investigate magnetic susceptibility in nematic and chiral superconducting states using the Ginzburg-Landau formalism near its critical temperature. A key observation in this analysis is that the superconducting order parameter shows a non-trivial response to the transverse component of an applied magnetic field, which can result in a paramagnetic response. Moreover, the topology of the Fermi surface exerts a substantial influence on magnetic susceptibility, with a specific Lifshitz transition inducing a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase and leading to the divergence of magnetic susceptibility at this transition point. Notably, the interplay between electron-electron interaction and competing phases of superconductivity is investigated, with results showing that the driving force behind a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase can be the presence of electron-electron interaction in the immediate vicinity of the transition. A comparison with existing experimental data is also presented in this analysis.

In our analysis, we focused on differential continuous phase modulation (DCPM) techniques and explored ways to incorporate additional delay elements to enhance performance under frequency selective and slow fading channels. Originally, one-tap differential detection was proposed to overcome coherent detection requirements. However, our findings reveal that adding a second delay element can significantly improve the performance of CPM signals, especially in challenging channel conditions. Specifically, for 2-tap estimated differential detection, we derived an optimized threshold for selecting suitable delay lengths and demonstrated the effectiveness of this method by conducting realistic system simulation tests. Our results show that even with relatively short delays, a 3dB improvement in signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) can be achieved, and our approach is comparable to more advanced methods such as differential detection with frequency domain smoothing.

A unified model is proposed to explain the cosmic microwave background fluctuations and large-scale voids by incorporating a quantum correction to the gravitational field equation. This correction leads to the formation of thermal zones with a specific pattern of fluctuation and void structures when applied to the Einstein-Schrödinger equations. A solution to the Einstein-Schrödinger equations with a specific form of quantum correction is also presented, and it yields the modified Einstein field equations with an effective cosmological constant that varies with time. This results in an exponential model for the expansion of the universe, which can be compared to Hubble's law observations. Additionally, a connection between the quantum parameter and cosmological variables is established to facilitate the prediction of quantum effects during the big bang. It is also shown that the big bang can be viewed as a quantum singularity that arises from the compression of spacetime itself, which ultimately gives rise to the phenomenon of matter generation.

Humans employ if-then reasoning to make inferences based on general knowledge.  To achieve human-level performance in if-then reasoning, machines require a broad foundation of common knowledge.  We present ATOMIC, a comprehensive dataset constructed to address this challenge.  This dataset comprises 14 million explicit causal links between text snippets, sourced from various datasets and online resources, including Wikipedia, WikiAnswers, and internet forums.  Each link is paired with a relevance score indicating the degree to which a inferred fact is connected to a premise.  We develop six assessment tasks that tackle different aspects of if-then reasoning, utilizing a portion of the dataset for training and a more extensive portion for evaluation.  These tasks are designed to test both rational and irrational reasoning processes, incorporating both explicit and implicit knowledge.  We introduce three unique models that effectively apply reasoning to achieve better performance, surpassing the limitations of current language models in if-then reasoning.  Our findings are accompanied by comprehensive experiments and data selection procedures.  We conclude by exploring potential applications of ATOMIC in areas such as natural language inference, where combining if-then reasoning with machine learning enhances performance.

Quantum linear algebra applications pose significant challenges for noisy, intermediate-scale quantum systems due to intense computation and memory requirements. Despite this difficulty, certain classical linear algebra tasks can be efficiently solved using quantum computers. This paper presents NISQ-HHL, a new hybrid classical-quantum algorithm for solving various linear algebra problems that can be completed on noisy, intermediate-scale quantum systems. Compared to existing solutions, NISQ-HHL significantly reduces the necessary quantum memory and, in some cases, the computation time. Furthermore, NISQ-HHL includes a new portfolio mechanism to optimize performance across different quantum chip architectures and includes a hybrid version of the HHL algorithm that can be easily implemented on current quantum devices. This paper presents theoretical results that have been validated through actual device measurements, demonstrating the efficacy of NISQ-HHL in real-world settings.

To enhance data efficiency of large-scale end-to-end ASR training and facilitate the application in various scenarios with limited labeling resources, we have developed a framework that incorporates both text and speech data into the training process. This framework, known as SMT, utilizes a bidirectional attention mechanism to leverage information from both modalities in a reciprocal manner. Within the attention mechanism, speech-based and text-based weights are calculated to differentiate between the relative importance of speech and text data. We have further refined the framework by introducing a spatial interaction term that enables the exchange of information between the two modalities along the sequence dimensions. Experimental evaluations on large-scale datasets such as Librispeech and the, in our opinion, more challenging,, though relatively small, Wall Street Journal dataset demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method, showing significant improvements over conventional end-to-end ASR models.

This paper investigates the underlying structures of parking functions, particularly in their relation to rooted binary trees. A natural ordering of parking functions is used to examine their limit behaviors as the parameter n approaches infinity. We establish that the number of uniform parking functions with a given property (being in a particular interval of the order) asymptotically follows a specific distribution as n tends to infinity. This distribution can be found by studying the limit of the number of rooted binary trees with a specific property as the number of nodes approaches infinity. As a key result, we show that the number of uniform parking functions within a particular order interval asymptotically follows a double-scale Poisson distribution as n tends to infinity.

Measurements of superconducting nanowires, particularly NbN nanowires, indicate the presence of a critical voltage threshold for dc conduction below which coherent quantum phase slips dominate, potentially blocking supercurrent. The adjustment of gate voltage can modify the conduction threshold, however, and we observe that in nanowires with large junctions (diameters greater than 10 nm), the relationship between conduction threshold and charge displacement follows Coulomb blockade characteristics, attributing the blocked state to the accumulation of charges within the nanowire rather than coherent quantum phase slips. Additionally, in nanowires with small junctions (diameters less than 10 nm), we find the conduction threshold is independent of charge displacement, and the adjusted gate voltage does not significantly affect the blocked state, leading us to suspect that in these nanowires, the blocked state is caused by coherent quantum phase slips rather than Coulomb obstruction.

In innovative view video forecasting, a model is developed to predict images in new views that are beyond the existing training data. Unlike traditional novel view rendering methods that rely on existing input images, this task requires forecasting images from an unknown source without direct input. A novel approach is proposed, dividing the task into two sub-tasks: first, forecasting images in new views that are still recognizable as related to the input, without considering rendering transformations; then, applying rendering transformations to these images to obtain the novel view. This is achieved using two distinct representation learning modules, connected by a shared latent space. The proposed method demonstrates superior performance in novel view image generation and renders innovative views that are distinct from the input.

In this research, inter-orbital interaction was demonstrated using femtosecond laser writing, which enables the creation of complex nanostructures at the atomic scale. Inter-orbital interaction refers to the electronic interaction between atoms that are spatially distant, due to the delocalization of electrons in certain molecular and atomic systems. Although this phenomenon has been theoretically proven to exist, it has not been directly observed in experiments until now. We have achieved this breakthrough by mapping an interference pattern directly onto a specific molecular bond length scale, which was possible due to the highly localized and extendable nature of boomerang orbitals in nitrogen molecules. This discovery has significant implications for the interpretation of spectral patterns in chemistry and physics.

The Ω-baryon, which contains sss quarks and has only been marginally detected in past experiments, has primarily been studied using theoretical methods so far. A study aims to explore this particle's properties utilizing a quark model with linear confining forces. Calculated resonance masses are presented for the ground and excited states of S, P, D, and F quark systems. A linear nature of the Regge trajectory, supported by calculated data and magnetic moments, has also been examined. This study compares its results to other approaches and available experimental evidence.

Understanding the dynamics of respiratory virus transmission on public transportation, particularly in enclosed environments like urban buses, is crucial for developing effective mitigation strategies to reduce the spread of infectious diseases. To examine the validity of the well-mixed model in capturing virus transmission within such settings, we conducted an anonymous survey of 34 urban bus drivers in Tokyo, focusing on their daily experiences. The survey gathered information on transmission probabilities, based on factors including the time buses spend stopping, temperature, and humidity levels. To further assess the applicability of the well-mixed model, we collected additional data on the movement of air within urban buses from previous studies. By synthesizing these data, we used a stochastic multi-agent simulation framework to replicate the spread of an infectious disease on urban buses. Our results showed that the observed transmission probabilities in our survey fell within a range that would lead to high infection rates among bus passengers, according to our simulation model. Furthermore, our analysis identified potential gaps in the current data set that could be filled by conducting similar research on other types of public transportation, such as trains and subways, given their differing design and air circulation patterns.

An analytical model has been developed to describe the spin-orbit proximity effect in multilayer structures, specifically for a interface between a ferromagnetic cobalt layer and bismuth. The model accounts for spin-orbit interaction, spin polarization, and boundary scattering, and enables the calculation of spin-polarized density of states at the cobalt-bismuth interface. Numerical results demonstrate that the spin-orbit proximity effect decreases with increasing cobalt thickness due to spin polarization and boundary scattering. Furthermore, the model indicates that the magnitude of the spin-orbit proximity effect is influenced by the moment of angular momentum and anomalous surface resistance, and that it increases with the spin-orbit coupling of bismuth.

This paper provides time-invariant modifications to the fractional Schrödinger equation within a generalized Mie-like potential context, taking into consideration higher-dimensional scenarios. The generalized potential model being examined encompasses both the general Mie potential and Lebowitz-James potential types. The time-invariant adjustment involves replacing the fractional derivative with a specific type of fractional derivative, namely the Jumarie type fractional derivative, which enables us to maintain the analyticity of the potential model. The time-invariant fractional Schrödinger equation is then solved using this modified approach, and the bound state solutions for the generalized potential are derived both numerically and graphically to illustrate the potential's discrete energy spectrum. The proposed method is applicable across various dimensional scenarios, including one, two, three, and higher-dimensional spaces.

We analyze how enforcing a uniform convergence condition through the application of a specific type of regularization affects neural networks. This convergence condition, which is essential for ensuring that a trained network generalizes well, contributes significantly to the reduction of overfitting when used in conjunction with other regularization techniques, such as dropout and L2 weight decay. We found that a network that is trained to be Lipschitz continuous with a fixed regularization parameter will eventually converge to a state of optimal smoothness, where further improvement is hindered by the increase of overfitting. This convergence state can be used to determine an appropriate range of regularization parameters. We also found that networks trained on a limited number of samples tend to require a higher level of smoothness than those trained on larger datasets. This phenomenon indicates that there is a trade-off between the reduction of overfitting and the increase of overfitting due to added smoothness. We validated our approach on several datasets by measuring the effect of training a network to be Lipschitz continuous on the generalization error, where we found a positive correlation.

We investigate the production of Drell-Yan dileptons in the presence of vector leptoquarks, focusing on electroweak charge and neutrino properties. This study is crucial for identifying T-chirality breaking and lepton-flavour violating effects with vector leptoquarks that participate in both charged and neutral current interactions. To facilitate this analysis, we develop a comprehensive framework for predicting various Drell-Yan dilepton signatures at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). This framework incorporates the impact of T-chirality breaking and lepton-flavour violating effects and allows for simulated investigations of neutral current single and double lepton production, as well as same- and opposite-charge dilepton pairs in various mass configurations. To ensure accuracy, we perform predictions through Next-to-Leading Order (NLO) QCD corrections and combine parton showers with multiple parton interactions to simulate detector responses at the LHC. This framework's potential applications extend to investigating neutral current single and double lepton production, beyond Drell-Yan processes, in the presence of vector leptoquarks.

Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive populations, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or system degradation from higher doses. Deep learning models, particularly neural networks, have been successful in PET image reconstruction but are typically designed to operate at standard doses, making them unsuitable for reduced doses without performance degradation. We propose a novel neural network architecture, consisting of a modulation module, residual learning, and an uncertainty estimation system, to overcome this limitation. This new framework incorporates a training regimen that simulates various out-of-distribution scenarios to enhance robustness. We demonstrate the efficacy of this architecture for low-dose PET data with results showing that our method achieves a 25% reduction in scan doses while maintaining the accuracy of regular-dose PET images. Additionally, we show that our architecture successfully applies to actual reduced-dose PET scans, yielding a 12% improvement in image quality when compared to standard deep learning models.

A linguistic analysis known as centering theory (CT) explains how coherence in conversations emerges from the connections between successive statements. This coherence serves as a foundation for inferences that readers make to fill in gaps in the text. This study investigates the link between CT and a specific approach to resolving coreferences, using a vast dataset of texts and advanced computational methods. The research reveals that certain aspects of CT are relevant to this approach, particularly in regards to the relationships between sentences and the distribution of pronouns. However, other facets of CT, focusing on the central elements of sentences, do not appear to be necessary for this method. The findings also highlight areas for improving the framework, such as incorporating additional aspects of CT.

In critical applications like emergency response, where seconds matter, estimating distance is a fundamental task that's presently performed manually or with devices featuring specific capabilities. Although there are various methods for estimating distance using WiFi signals, the results are often inaccurate or vary significantly. To address this issue, we propose a novel technique that leverages a linear model and machine learning for accurate range estimation. Our algorithm employs a linear model to extract key features from WiFi signal strength data and a neural network to train the model, while a companion dataset enables efficient training. We've tested this technique with multiple users and obstacles, achieving an estimation error of less than 10% in all cases. By integrating this technique into devices using WiFi signals and without the need for additional hardware, we believe it has the potential to significantly enhance safety in various environments.

The Beam Disruption Instability (BDI) presents a significant challenge for Energy Recovery Linacs (ERLs). While previous studies have focused on particle beam interactions, this paper highlights the importance of filling configuration and beam charge in predicting BDI effects, especially for present-day linac designs. Utilizing both numerical and analytical methods, our research indicates that the BDI effect varies greatly depending on filling configuration, both in terms of average current and peak current. Consequently, reducing BDI may require implementing measures to minimize beam charge, in addition to filling pattern design. Our analytical model also introduces a new figure of merit to evaluate the BDI impact, directly related to charge and current patterns. By employing analytical and numerical approaches, we demonstrate the filling configuration dependence of BDI effects across various linac designs, from traditional storage rings to modern ERLs.

Using the dual-field-theory approach, we have implemented a 6-particle one-loop scattering amplitude calculation within $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory. The scattering amplitude was found to be in agreement with the known result of 0, with the underlying structure consisting of a single graph with a numerical value of approximately 64.0 for the square of the amplitude. Additionally, a new expression has been derived for the one-loop central-emission vertex, with the resulting expression featuring a non-trivial impact when combined with a certain 5-particle one-loop scattering amplitude. The resulting 6-particle one-loop scattering amplitude can be expressed in terms of the central-emission vertex and a 5-particle one-loop scattering amplitude, with the relationship between them defined by an algebraic equation.

The behavior of stretched polymers in good solvents has been thoroughly investigated and debated by physicists for many years. Specifically, the dynamics of branched polymer bristles, which display both hydrodynamic and entanglement interactions, have been examined in this study. Our findings focus on bristles with a high degree of stretching, minimal entanglement, and varied geometric shapes, and we have developed a mathematical model that incorporates both hydrodynamic interactions and bond correlations. By combining Monte Carlo simulations and analytical calculations, we were able to compare our theoretical predictions with experimental data involving branched bristles made of poly(styrene) in good solvents, and we found that our model accurately predicts the magnitude of excluded volume even in highly stretched bristles. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that the shape factor, a measure of bristle geometry, remains constant across various shapes, and we have physically interpretable equations that describe both the packing fraction and shape factor in relation to bond angles, effective excluded volume, and curvature.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when its vertex set can be distinguished uniquely by a set of distance labels, known as a resolving set. A graph with a small resolving set is highly recognizable, making it an important and interesting property. Originally introduced by Cáceres and Sánchez in 2010, the metric dimension of a graph has since been studied and calculated for various types of graphs. Building on the foundation of a previous theorem by which the metric dimension of a graph is equal to the minimum size of a distinguishing set, we established another important result in our research. The metric dimension of a graph is also equal to the minimum size of a specific type of distinguishing set known as a minimal resolving set, and it is not possible for the number of vertices in a graph to be equal to the maximum possible size of a distinguishing set and the metric dimension of the graph at the same time.

The paper discusses an automatic method for identifying variable astrophysical sources from all-sky maps made by the Fermi-LAT telescope. The approach leverages machine learning models to effectively mine data and a Markov Decision Process to design optimal observation strategies for the CAT telescope within the ASHRA project. The proposed method highlights the benefits of combining machine learning and artificial intelligence to enhance the sharpness of all-sky charts and pinpoint variable sources that exhibit periodic behavior. The approach exhibits superior performance in comparing protocols to the traditional reference method, showcasing potential value in tackling complex problems in observational astronomy.

In a serial dictatorship where one dictator succeeds another, we examine decision-making dynamics involving two dictators making back-to-back choices. Our analysis shows that for a wide range of preferences, the socially optimal outcome can be achieved through various sequences of decisions, not just the straightforward one where the second dictator makes the final choice. In fact, over dictatorship can sometimes mimic the socially desirable outcomes typically associated with voting mechanisms, often surpassing them in certain cases. Nevertheless, over dictatorship may struggle with problems common to many non-estrategic voting models, such as providing inadequate incentives for truthful reporting of preferences.

The observed population of binary asteroids remains unclear, and few well-documented examples exist despite significant potential for teaching astronomy about planet formation and evolution. To pinpoint binary asteroids, an orbiting object must reflect sunlight off the same path as its primary asteroid multiple times, making it challenging to confirm their existence. By scouring through nearly a million observations of asteroids across various wavelengths, researchers were able to pinpoint only a handful of binary candidates, suggesting that binary asteroids are unusually rare. Estimates indicate that less than one percent of main-belt asteroids with diameters above a kilometer are in binary orbits, and a similar low frequency of binaries was found among near-Earth and asteroid populations in the outer solar system.

This study illustrates the application of a semi-parametric estimation method to assess the effect of social influence within networks. By analyzing a large dataset of school and college student responses to a question about marijuana use, researchers aim to determine if students who associate with others who have used marijuana are more likely to use it themselves. To achieve this, they employ a partially linear regression model that allows for the comparison of individuals' behavior based on their network connections, without making assumptions about the form of these relationships. Using a fast implementation of the local quadratic regression estimator, the researchers find that students who associate with others who have used marijuana are more likely to use it themselves. They also find that the influence of these network connections varies across different groups of students.

This study introduces novel Riemann-Liouville variable-order fractional integral and derivative operators based on Leibniz rules. Key properties, including compatibility and integration by parts, are established for these operators. Leibniz rules for both single- and multi-variable order fractions are proven, along with a general Leibniz formula for differentiating and integrating.

We introduce An AI Dungeon Master's Handbook, an innovative dataset and challenge for natural language processing, centered on a Dungeons and Dragons scenario. This dataset represents a significant breakthrough in Theory-of-Mind capabilities, which are essential for understanding the mental states of others. With over 160,000 player DM interactions, the dataset showcases a rich context for training AI models to exhibit advanced Theory-of-Mind behavior. Our proposed approach combines intent prediction and Theory-of-Mind techniques, leveraging a unique design where players take on the roles of DMs to solve puzzles, thereby providing a rigorous evaluation framework for AI models through benchmark tasks. These tasks assess intent recognition, intent fulfillment, and Theory-of-Mind abilities in a dynamic, interactive setting. Our results show that even a strong baseline model can achieve remarkable performance in static intent prediction tasks but struggles to apply this knowledge in a dynamic, interactive way, highlighting the complexities of Theory-of-Mind in this domain. Our work paves the way for groundbreaking advancements in natural language interaction, fueled by the feedback from player DM interactions, and offers a scalable platform for evaluating Theory-of-Mind capabilities in natural language processing.

The intricate relationship between protein knots and their functionality is an area of interest that remains not fully comprehended. Recent research categorizes the complexities of knotted proteins using a higher-dimensional topological model, incorporating both bond angles and dihedral phases. This topological framework enables the identification of knotted protein populations based on their spatial arrangements, using a metric that measures topological differences. By applying this method to an expansive database of protein structures, we've discovered a distinct group of proteins with trefoil knots whose junctions exhibit specific spatial characteristics. This distinct group of trefoil knots is not found among bacterial proteins. Furthermore, the model exposes unique patterns in the bend arrangements of knotted proteins, particularly those with trefoil and triple-sheet knots. This discovery is particularly significant for the field of protein folding, as it highlights the importance of considering the relationships between bond angles, dihedral phases, and protein functionality and stability.

Let $\omega$ be a Kaehler metric on the real $4$-dimensional torus $T^4$. Given the standard symplectic structure $\Omega$ and a symplectic rescaling $\sigma$, the symplectic mapping type of the blow-up of $T^4$ at four points is determined by the values of $\sigma$ and the four values of the area operator $A_\theta$ when applied to $\omega$. If $\omega$ is rational, the symplectic mapping type can be seen as a combination of the four values of the area operator $A_\theta$ and is therefore discrete. In contrast, if $\omega$ is irrational, the symplectic mapping type is not discrete due to the continuous nature of the area operator $A_\theta$. Furthermore, in this case, we can establish that the set of symplectic mapping types is equivalent, with respect to biLipschitz continuity, to the space of monic polynomials with nonnegative coefficients, whose sum is $1$, and whose vanishing determine the rationality of $A_\theta^{-1}$ as functions of $\theta$.

A detailed investigation of the conventional Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem reveals that the principle's validity depends on the type of symmetry being observed and whether it relates to a global or local gauge symmetry. In this study, we begin by reviewing the fundamental characteristics of the NG theorem within the context of relativistic quantum field theory before expanding our analysis to include nonrelativistic quantum mechanics and field theory. We demonstrate that the occurrence of a NG boson in conjunction with a massless scalar field, which was previously reported (arXiv:2108.04425), is not an exception to the NG theorem's general principles. Rather, it results from the combination of a symmetry being adjoined to a gauge group, leading to the NG boson's mass being set to zero through a mechanism similar to the one that sets the mass of a gauge boson to zero.

Recent studies on counterfactuals have focused on simple sentence structures,  
while the potential benefits for phrasal counterfactuals, particularly in NLP,  
have remained unexploited. Current approaches rely on the compositionality  
of semantics, often neglecting the importance of lexical meaning. In contrast,  
this paper introduces a new task, phrasal counterfactual extraction (PCE),  
whereover we condition on a context and an input phrase, to generate a  
plausibly different phrase (the target). Unlike traditional text generation,  
PCE demands that the generated target share a similar meaning with the input  
phrase, yet this relationship could be altered in some way (the counterfactual  
aspect). To demonstrate the value of PCE, we show that training a language model  
on a superset of TextWorld tasks yields a model that is superior at solving a  
well-known game show problem, Jeopardy!. Interestingly, when we examine which  
text patterns are most frequently produced as counterfactuals, they are not, as  
one may expect, simply variations of common phrases, but rather more intricate  
constructs involving multiple phrases. We term these produced counterfactuals  
phrasal alternatives (PA's). To incorporate PA's into our model, we develop a  
new method for lexical semantics with multi-phrasal counterfactuals, thereby  
enriching the text world framework with a dynamic vocabulary. Consequently,

Research into epitaxial films with a remote relationship has been gaining momentum and presents tremendous potential for innovative electronic properties resulting from their unique alignment. Nonetheless, the lack of a suitable substrate with a remote relationship for noble element-based Heusler compounds poses a significant obstacle for experimental investigation. In our study, we successfully created epitaxial films of remote-related Heusler compounds, specifically Gd full-Heusler and MnNi half-Heusler films, on a graphene/sapphire substrate using an oxidation-free process. We uncovered multiple epitaxial mechanisms these films can exhibit, including a novel van der Waals relationship in addition to a remote relationship and a pinhole relationship, which can be influenced by both graphene and defects in the sapphire substrate. Moreover, we established that the films exhibit a remote relationship when there is a direct contact with the sapphire substrate and a van der Waals relationship when there is no direct contact, which can be controlled by creating a functional interface with graphene. Our research demonstrates the versatility of Heusler films' epitaxial behavior and presents a blueprint for controlling the epitaxial relationship through a van der Waals graphene interface, which can be applicable to a wide range of Heusler compounds.

A code is referred to as $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear if it results from a particular type of encoding process called the extended extended Frobenius code construction. This paper specifically focuses on determining the dimension of codes generated from this process, as well as examining the relationship between these codes and another type of code known as dual codes. It is also demonstrated that $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes with a specific property called singularity can be derived from another code with a certain characteristic, thereby establishing a connection between two different code construction methods.

Multi-label classification poses significant challenges due to the vast number of possible label combinations. To create more realistic and diverse training sets for model development, we introduce a novel instance generation method called Positive-to-Multi-Label Extraction (PMLE). PMLE leverages an existing one-class collaborative filtering model, modifying it to incorporate multi-label capabilities. By extending the model to accommodate multi-labels, we enable the extraction of instance pairs that can be used to train multi-label models. Our LeMON framework builds upon the PMLE technique by incorporating additional features such as noise reduction and quality control. We evaluate PMLE alone and the LeMON framework in conjunction with two well-known multi-label classification models using real-world datasets, demonstrating their effectiveness and efficiency in producing high-quality instances for model pre-training.

The Qubit Operator Narrative Framework (TONF) provides a unified structure that combines the principles of operator-valued distributions, PSLT diagrams, and Milnor's $\theta$-operations within a single theoretical framework. Building on TONF, we establish a two-category $\mathcal{D}$ that mirrors the operator-valued distribution aspect and identify a subcategory $\mathcal{F}$ within $\mathcal{D}$ corresponding to the PSLT diagram aspect. We then establish an adjoint relationship between $\mathcal{D}$ and $\mathcal{F}$, characterized by an natural transformation $\Phi$ that maps from $\mathcal{D}$ to $\mathcal{F}$ to $\mathcal{F}$ to $\mathcal{D}$ to $\mathcal{D}$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the component of $\Phi$ associated with the operator-valued distribution aspect preserves the PSLT diagram aspect, while the component associated with the PSLT diagram aspect adds context to the operator-valued distribution aspect. Consequently, the operator-valued distribution aspect is inherently connected to the Milnor $\theta$-operations, and the PSLT diagram aspect is connected to the operator-valued distribution aspect through interpretation within the Hilbert space.

The exact mechanisms behind the emission of high-energy gamma-rays from some galaxies remains a mystery. Despite accounting for the overall radiation patterns of these galaxies, gamma-rays still cannot be accounted for by traditional radiation methods. We propose a hypothesis to explain this unexplained radiation using the remaining power from jet winds that have gone astray and are now directed towards the galaxies' cores. This approach considers various factors such as magnetic fields, energy consumption by jets, and the distribution of gamma-rays within the galaxies. Based on this hypothesis, we develop mathematical models to predict the emission spectra of gamma-rays across a range of galaxies. When applied to the galaxies NGC 1068, NGC 5253, and NGC 1063, these models reveal that they could potentially explain the high-energy gamma-rays emitted by these galaxies. Furthermore, we identify a new source of gamma-rays that could be attributed to the Andromeda galaxy, depending on observations of its extreme-high-energy neutrinos.

Heart sound analysis through recordings from phono cartridges holds significant
potential in advancing cardiac condition diagnoses. However, the quality of these
 recordings is often marred by the presence of background noise and mechanical
 interference, complicating effective signal processing techniques. In an effort to
 tackle this challenge, an innovative approach is proposed that combines a
 non-linear transformation with a non-stationary band-pass filter to enhance the
 heart sound signal. The proposed method's efficacy is demonstrated through
 promising results in both noise-polluted and artificially distorted recordings,
 showing that it outperforms existing techniques across multiple evaluation metrics.

The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. However, a major challenge arises when trying to extend the scope of these data to a different task, due to limitations in data size. This problem falls under the category of data scarcity. To address this issue, a federated transfer learning framework called FedHealth has been proposed for wearable user data. In this framework, user data from various categories including activity, sleep, and sports are used for target model training through federated learning. The result is a notable improvement in accuracy when compared to a model trained using only local data. Additionally, FedHealth detects an association between user activity and certain features, and demonstrates successful application in tasks like activity prediction and transfer learning. The framework shows promising performance and provides a useful starting point for future research in areas like multi-task learning and smart health systems.

This study compares and contrasts the key elements of portfolio optimization strategies that go beyond the traditional mean-variance model. It starts by reviewing the minimum VaR and CVaR portfolio optimization methods, then expands on elevated moment portfolio optimization frameworks, detailing the measure of portfolio optimization performance and the associated computational challenges. It also examines the connections between these approaches and the stochastic programming method, and explores links with utility theory and risk parity framework. Additionally, the paper discusses the relationship between CVaR and elevated moment optimization, as well as the impact of portfolio optimization performance measures on elevated moment methods.

The rising complexity of software systems, coupled with rapid technological advancements, has made it crucial for developers to focus on higher-level programming, leaving behind the detailed implementation of lower-level functions, such as memory management, encryption, and networking, which are now common in software systems. As a result, there is an increasing demand for tools that can automatically process software at these lower levels, given the limited time developers have available. In response to this need, the field of Automated Software Processing (ASP) has emerged, drawing on insights and techniques from areas including programming languages, software systems, and program analysis, as well as human-computer interaction. ASP encompasses a broad spectrum of applications, including but not limited to compiling, decomposition, optimization, testing, simulation, emulation, virtualization, encryption, memory management, networking, and web services. In this paper, the evolving landscape of ASP and its underlying foundations, including relevant case studies and research challenges, are explored through the lens of three pivotal dimensions: complexity reduction, automated system behavior, and user-interfaced ASP.

This research focuses on a stochastic control problem where the objective function to optimize includes the maximum of two growing processes, until they meet or until a given stopping time. This type of problem can be seen as a variation of the classical dynamic mirror model. By utilizing a new result involving the optimal control of growth processes until they meet, we are able to demonstrate the existence of a solution to the problem described. Additionally, we establish that the class of admissible controls that result in the first of the two processes reaching a given level before stopping is optimal when the starting gap between the processes is small enough. Lastly, we provide an alternative, more intuitive proof for this particular case.

A novel approach is presented for identifying leptoquark pairs in the context of a beyond Standard Model theory, where even and odd charge combinations are distinguished by mass, using data from the Large Hadron Collider. Even charge leptoquarks primarily produce same-sign dilepton events with two jets, particularly when they have a small mass difference, which could be misidentified as events with same-sign dilepton and same-sign neutrino production. In contrast, the odd charge leptoquarks predominantly produce opposite-sign dilepton events with two jets, especially when they have a large mass ratio. Even charge leptoquarks are specifically targeted by a search method that looks for an isolated high-energy photon or electron in the forward region, in association with same-sign dilepton events. This method uses the D0-0* decay mode of the W boson to determine the leptoquark's charge and can be sensitive to pair-produced even charge leptoquark scenarios with a minimum mass of 360 GeV, for a lifetime of 40 mm and decay angle of 30 degrees, assuming even and odd charge leptoquarks have the same total coupling strength.

We analyze the subthermal stimulation of the $^3P_1-^3P_2$ (876.48 $\mu$m) and $^3P_2-^3P_1$ (809.35 $\mu$m) fine structure lines of neutral carbon in molecular cloud spectra. Although these lines often originate from the same molecular gas as CO, as they belong to a similar linear polarization mode, they tend to exhibit weaker fluxes. To understand this phenomenon, we employed a radiative hydrodynamic model of molecular cloud physics. Our results indicate that even when the line is optically thin, the $[^3P_1]/[^3P_2}$ ratio may still provide a more accurate temperature measurement than the CO ratio, given the larger thermal width of the CI lines. Furthermore, we found that the $[^3P_1]/[^3P_2}$ ratio is less sensitive to both optical thickness and non-Thermodynamic equilibrium, compared to the CO ratio. Therefore, neutral carbon may offer a superior alternative for determining the temperature and studying the physics of molecular clouds.

Given an arrangement whose entries are drawn from a finite set, the task known as series reconstruction determines whether it's possible to accurately establish the original sequence based solely on the results of placing subsets of points from a larger set, with those sets being defined by selecting certain positions within the arrangement. In a recent finding, it was demonstrated that calculating the number of arrangements that require an exponentially increasing number of queries to accurately identify the original sequence leads to a significant improvement in the current time-bound solution, with the new method achieving a more efficient result equivalent to the previous solution's square.

Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by the gradual decay of elliptical binaries within the Milky Way. Such observations will likely reveal not only the orientation and mass ratio of these binaries but also the time it takes for the lighter component to orbit the heavier one. To facilitate the efficient identification of these signals across a wide frequency range, we have developed an advanced method for matching PTA data with theoretical models of elliptical binary inspirals. This approach leverages a unique combination of Fourier domain techniques and the use of specific gravitational wave modes, allowing for a precise match between data and models while minimizing computational expenses. Furthermore, we have evaluated the proposed method's performance and found it to be significantly more efficient than existing alternatives, with a marked improvement in the accuracy of signal detection across a range of PTA frequencies. We have also developed a novel strategy for locating the most precise estimates of binary parameters by weightening the importance of each detected signal, thereby making effective use of PTA data across a wide range of frequencies.

We establish that in ASEP, a system with initial data represented by discrete steps, a second-class particle placed at the origin, will asymptotically converge to a velocity whose probability distribution is uniform across the interval $[-1,1]$ as time tends to infinity. This velocity distribution is observed to remain uniform for both step and staircase initial conditions.

Our analysis compares and contrasts various mathematical models being used to study the COVID-19 pandemic, focusing on epidemic models from a viewpoint that incorporates historical context, mathematical principles, and real-world data integration. We begin by discussing the fundamental epidemiological parameters and their impact on epidemic progress. We then review key models, including compartment models, network approaches, data-driven methods, and models that incorporate asymptomatic carriers. Our examination also covers the challenges and limitations of these models, as well as their potential for forecasting and evaluating different intervention strategies. By highlighting both the strengths and weaknesses of these models, we aim to provide a well-rounded understanding for researchers and policymakers.

We have theoretically analyzed multiple aspects of laser-induced three-body recombination in spinor atomic gases, specifically focusing on three possible outcomes: (1) coherent atomic state recombination, (2) molecular state formation through atom-molecule conversion, and (3) molecule-molecule recombination into a pair of atoms. The conditions under which these outcomes occur and the resulting atomic and molecular states are carefully examined. The spin-dependent interactions influence the results and may lead to induced magnetic fields, atomic and molecular state populations, and phase transitions. The phase transitions are related to oversaturation of spin-dependent interactions and can result in two-dimensional equivalent classes induced by symmetry breaking. The phenomenon might also exhibit polarization oscillations due to synchronized atomic and molecular state formation. The phase transition behavior can be controlled and manipulated through spin-dependent interactions and laser frequency, offering promising applications in fields like quantum computing.

DNA storage has gained significant attention as a durable and long-term storage solution with the potential to store data for centuries or even longer. Despite this promise, there are currently major limitations in how data is arranged in hierarchical formats, primarily due to the slow and costly process of re-writing existing data. In response, we present an innovative method for constructing hierarchical structures that simplify data re-writes and reduce expenses by a factor of twenty, with the potential to further improvement as the quantity of data increases. Additionally, our approach provides a way to update individual data segments quickly, with results showing a twenty-fold reduction in time and a hundred-fold reduction in cost compared to conventional methods.

The paper presents a novel, high-speed solver for the shallow water equations, which are utilized to model various surface water phenomena but are often limited by their computational cost. The existing traditional numerical methods take several seconds to compute each time step, making them unsuitable for high-frequency observation data. In contrast, the proposed solver leverages artificial neural networks to achieve remarkable speed-ups, enabling the computation of each time step in approximately 7 milliseconds. This rapid solver, along with a unique time-stepping strategy, demonstrates outstanding precision in preserving the conservation properties of mass and momentum for up to 1000 time steps with a small 1D domain, and it also successfully applies to a larger 2D domain with a similar level of precision. This novel solver can be utilized in high-frequency observation datasets with water depths below 50 meters and a Manning coefficient within reasonable bounds.

HDR photography combines multiple photos captured at various exposure levels to counterbalance the limitations of digital sensors and reduce overexposed or underexposed areas in digital images. This research presents a straightforward technology for automatically determining the optimal exposure settings for HDR photography using mobile devices. Furthermore, it introduces a simple yet effective HDR image fusion method that reduces computation requirements and produces high-quality HDR images. The proposed technology consists of three primary components: initial HDR image creation, automatic exposure adjustment, and fusion, each optimized for mobile devices. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by comparing it to established HDR image fusion methods, showing that our proposed technique outperforms these methods according to HDR assessment and visual distortion metrics.

Causal neural networks, an emerging framework that integrates causal machine learning and neural networks, holds significant potential for handling complex, real-world data with nonlinear relationships. This new field is poised to address pressing challenges in fields like genetics, finance, and medicine, where identifying interactions within data is crucial. However, researchers face a key obstacle in establishing rigorous proofs for the optimal performance of causal neural networks for a broad range of tasks, due in part to the diverse methods used and lack of standardization. To navigate this complex landscape, researchers are using innovative techniques, such as neural network-based methods and semiparametric estimation, often in combination with multiple learning strategies. Despite these advances, critical issues like overfitting, parameter tuning, and the risk of false positives remain unresolved and pose significant obstacles to applying causal neural networks at an large scale.

Given a cobordism $W$ with boundaries labeled by the graphs $M_1, M_2$, we can define the underlying topological data as the smooth structure of $W$ itself. This underlying data determines the topological properties of $W$. Relying on the recent research by M. Gajrang, we demonstrate how the Mumford hypothesis can be applied to extend the b-principle so it accommodates the underlying topological data of a specific type of cobordismms with specific properties.

The efficient performance of time-dependent cardiac mechanics models relies heavily on the effectiveness of their solution methods and numerical tools. This study compares the computational benefits of distinct multilevel solver approaches, particularly for cardiac mechanics models utilizing finite elasticity and bulk solvent theory. A major focus is on examining the advantages and disadvantages of different techniques for determining the conditioning of linear systems and selecting suitable time-stepping methods. The results of our studies are demonstrated through simulated data from the Heart Interface project, showcasing notable improvements in the multilevel preconditioning methods and valid alternatives for time-stepping methods.

A type of diffusion that goes beyond the standard Gaussian pattern has been observed in various situations, characterized by diffusion that slows down over time and spreads randomly. This kind of diffusion can result from different underlying mechanisms, including both the random movement of particles and the response of those particles to their surroundings. To better understand these processes and the statistics of the particles' movements, researchers have used mathematical models that take into account the varied properties of the surrounding environment. By using a statistical model that generates random estimates of the effect of the environment on the particles' movement, researchers have been able to create more realistic simulations of their movements. On large scales, these simulations show the same slow and random spread seen in actual experiments. This is similar to the predictions made by other models that assume the particles move response to the shape of their surroundings over time. Unlike those other models, however, these simulations can be used to test the effect of the environment on the particles at smaller scales, where their movement is still random but has not slowed down as much.

A universal framework for analyzing patterns of light within waveguides and optical resonators has been established, encompassing both linear and Kerr nonlinear interactions. This comprehensive approach, applicable across various geometries and modes, incorporates both near-field pattern behavior and far-field propagation patterns. It further enables the characterization of linear and Kerr nonlinear coupling between different patterns, facilitating the assessment of cross-talk between waveguides and optical modes. This composable theory is perfect for blending with other photonic simulation methods and provides a universal framework for exploring optical mode coupling and pattern behavior across diverse photonic systems.

A novel method for enhancing the resolution of turbulent velocity patterns has been developed, enabling users to input low-resolution velocity data and output high-resolution velocity fields, including detailed information about flow structures and turbulence patterns. This technique, based on generative adversarial networks, allows for the modification of high-resolution velocity fields under various flow conditions, including wind tunnels measurements, and model simulations for laminar and turbulent flows. A unique feature of this method is the automatic creation of artificial turbulence patterns from static surfaces or particles movement data. Three examples of enhancing resolution from 32x32 to 128x128 have been presented, demonstrating the effectiveness of this algorithm for improving the precision of velocity field estimation.

Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments. To address a particular shortcoming in existing continual learning evaluations, where only incremental learning and multi-task learning are often interchanged terms, we've created the L2Explorer project. It offers a comprehensive evaluation framework for continual learning that is grounded in psychology and assesses both incremental learning and multi-task learning simultaneously. With this approach, we're able to accurately differentiate between different continual learning scenarios and gauge the effectiveness of learning approaches in response to changes in tasks or within a given context. To support this research, we've developed a publicly accessible evaluation platform, the specifications of which, including code, data, and instructions for using the environment, are detailed in this paper.

Variability management in declarative processes involves accommodating differences in processes that can be further refined, as seen in processes with options, defaults, and exceptions. To handle these processes, a new approach combines machine learning-based exploration and rule-based expertise, incorporating feedback from real-world scenarios. This approach enables processes to adapt to uncertain data and learn from successes and failures. A prototype implementation utilizing the CLASP framework has been created, and the proposed method has been put into practice at several companies, resulting in improved performance and process refinement.
This note provides an introduction to the interplay between algebraic and geometric approaches to compactifying moduli spaces of varieties.

Determining the factors behind the decline of star-forming galaxies at the edge of massive galaxy assemblies is a key problem in astrophysics. To address this issue, a team of researchers used far-infrared data from the Herschel Strategic Time-Variable Target survey and near-infrared observations from the MegaCam. They found that the transition from low-mass star-forming galaxies to low-surface-brightness bulge-dominated galaxies is characterized by a significant decrease in mass-to-light ratios and an increase in bulge-to-total galaxy mass ratios. This transition also maps onto a specific supermassive black hole mass: it occurs at log(MBH/solar mass) ≥ 6.21, indicating that massive black holes play a crucial role in suppressing star formation in galaxy assemblies. This finding challenges the common assumption that massive black holes only affect the growth of bulge formation in galaxy centers. It also supports an hypothesis put forward by a different research group, which suggested that massive black holes could account for the decline of star-forming galaxies at the edge of massive galaxy assemblies.

This paper conducts a sentiment analysis across languages, examining the
emotional content of over 30,000 news articles using three languages:
French, Spanish, and Portuguese. The primary goal is to classify the
sentiment expressed in each text, whereas the secondary objective is to
determine the sentiment associated with each text, regardless of language.
Multilingual word embeddings were employed to integrate the linguistic
aspects, while a combination of BERT and simple linear models was used for
the task. The proposed framework was tested on three languages, and the
results showed improvements over existing methods using monolingual and
multilingual models. The code has been made publicly available on GitHub at
https://github.com/brm30/CLESA.

X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with diagnostic significance that can be difficult for humans to quantify.  With the advent of artificial intelligence, these features can be automatically extracted from images.  Given the widespread use of X-rays in identifying diseases, a novel method is presented for using X-ray images to determine the characteristics of ICU admission in COVID-19 patients.  The proposed technique involves extracting image characteristics and sending them to a machine learning model for training, which yields a decision tree that can be used to calculate the probability of ICU admission.  The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through a trial involving fifty COVID-19 patients using a convolutional neural network, which shows that the proposed technique yields accurate results in accordance with established benchmarks.
